script.text: Scientists say they found blood chemistry in a dinosaur bone. Does it hold up?

A study in the journal PNAS reports traces of heme, the iron molecule that helps blood carry oxygen, in a leg bone of a dinosaur named Aratasaurus. The animal lived in Brazil about one hundred fifteen million years ago.

The team, led by Curtin University, also saw tiny oval shapes inside the bone's blood vessel channels. They interpret them as fossilized red blood cells. They suggest fast burial with little oxygen helped preserve them. The authors do not claim that intact blood or proteins survived.

Not everyone agrees. Paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved, accepts the chemistry. But she says the shapes are dented and small, unlike typical red blood cells. So the cell claim stays disputed.
Will other labs confirm dinosaur blood cells? Yes or no?

upload.title: Dinosaur Bone May Hold Traces of Blood, Study Says #shorts
upload.description:
A PNAS study led by Curtin University reports heme molecules and oval structures, interpreted as fossilized red blood cells, in a 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus bone from Brazil. Outside experts such as Mary Schweitzer accept the chemistry but dispute that the shapes are cells.

Sources: PNAS paper (Grice et al.), Sci.News, CTV News, LiveScience, Nautilus.
